pos: a. (happening without previous notice; coming unexpectedly)
etymology: Old French sodain, from Latin subitaneus, from subire, to come up stealthily, from sub-, under, and ire, to go. What is sudden has come up from underneath — it was on its way while nobody was watching.
biblical_def: The word occurs three times, and each concerns fear or ruin arriving without notice. Eliphaz uses it as an accusation against Job: “Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee” (Job 22:10) — the false logic that a man's terror proves his guilt. Solomon uses it as a promise to the believer: “Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it cometh” (Pro 3:25). Note that Solomon does not deny the desolation is coming; he forbids the fear of it. And Paul uses it of the end: “For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape” (1Th 5:3). The figure is exact. Travail is sudden in its onset and entirely predictable in its coming; a woman nine months along is not surprised that labour exists, only that it has started now. So the day of the Lord is sudden only to those who were not counting — “the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night” (1Th 5:2) — and the same chapter tells believers they are not in darkness, that that day should overtake them as a thief.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sudden as happening without previous notice; coming unexpectedly or without the common preparatives; hasty; violent; rash; precipitate.
webster_full: SUD'DEN, a. [Fr. soudain; L. subitaneus, from subeo, to come upon.]
1. Happening without previous notice; coming unexpectedly, or without the common preparatives.
And sudden fear troubleth thee. Job 22.
2. Hasty; violent; rash; precipitate; passionate.
3. Hastily prepared or employed; quick; rapid. On a sudden, sooner than was expected; without the usual preparatives.
scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 5:3
For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape.
Proverbs 3:25
Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it cometh.
Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee;
1 Thessalonians 5:2
For yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night.
corruption_summary: Date-setting turns a sudden day into a scheduled one, while practical unbelief treats a promised day as one that will not come at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational prophecy charts, the recurring rapture dates, and the whole industry of end-times calculation exist to make the sudden day predictable, and they fail every time because Scripture has said they must. As a thief in the night is not a coded hint; it is a denial that the hour can be plotted. The dictionary rejects the nineteenth-century dispensational scheme as a novelty unknown to any Reformation confession, and it rejects the date-setting that scheme keeps generating. What Paul gives instead is not a calendar but a character: children of light, watching and sober, for whom the day is not a surprise even though the hour is unknown.

The far commoner corruption is the one Paul actually names, and it is not a doctrinal error but a mood: when they shall say, Peace and safety. It belongs to people who are not thinking about the matter at all. Proverbs 3:25 gives the believer's posture between the two ditches — not calculating and not complacent, but simply unafraid, because the desolation of the wicked is not his portion. And the figure of travail is the mercy in the passage: a birth is a terrible pain that ends in a living child, which is precisely how Scripture describes the day for those who belong to Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew pith'om (H6597), suddenly, in an instant; pachad (H6343), dread, sudden fear; Greek aiphnidios (G160), unexpected; Latin subire, to come up stealthily.
roots_lines: Hebrew pachad pith'om (H6343, H6597) — sudden dread; Proverbs 3:25 and Job 22:10, the same pairing in both.
Greek aiphnidios olethros (G160, G3639) — sudden ruin; 1 Thessalonians 5:3, the destruction that arrives unannounced.
Greek odin (G5604) — a birth pang; the figure Paul chooses, sudden in onset and certain in coming.
Greek kleptes en nukti (G2812) — a thief in the night; 1 Thessalonians 5:2, and the same figure in 2 Peter 3:10.
Latin subire, from sub- and ire — to go up from underneath; Webster's root, a thing already on its way.
usage: “When they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction” — and the saying is the symptom.
“Be not afraid of sudden fear” — the desolation is not denied; the fear is forbidden.
“As travail upon a woman with child” — sudden in onset, certain in coming.

pos: a. (pressing; importunate; calling for immediate attention or action)
etymology: Latin urgens, pressing, from urgere, to press, drive, or urge. The word is physical before it is temporal — it describes a force pushing, not merely a matter that is due soon.
biblical_def: Twice in the Authorized Version, and both times a pagan power is pressing hard on the people of God — in one case to expel them, in the other to kill them. The first is the night of the Passover: “And the Egyptians were urgent upon the people, that they might send them out of the land in haste; for they said, We be all dead men” (Exo 12:33). The nation that had refused to let Israel go through ten plagues now cannot get them out fast enough, and it is the Egyptians who are urgent. Pharaoh spent a year resisting and lost the argument in a night. The second is Babylon: “Therefore because the king's commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego” (Dan 3:22). The king's urgency overheated the furnace, and the haste killed his own soldiers while the three Hebrews walked in it unharmed. In both places human urgency is a form of loss of control, and in both it accomplishes God's purpose rather than the urgent man's. Against it stands the settled answer the three had already given: “But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines urgent as pressing with importunity; calling for immediate attention; instantly important; and vehement, earnest.
webster_full: UR'GENT, a. [L. urgens, from urgeo, to press.]
Pressing with importunity; calling for immediate attention; instantly important.
The affair is urgent.
The Egyptians were urgent upon the people. Ex. 12.
Vehement; earnest; importunate. Because the king's commandment was urgent. Dan. 3.
scriptures: Exodus 12:33
And the Egyptians were urgent upon the people, that they might send them out of the land in haste; for they said, We be all dead men.
Daniel 3:22
Therefore because the king's commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Daniel 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Psalm 2:4
He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.
corruption_summary: Urgency is treated as evidence of importance, and the church has learned to be governed by whatever is loudest and soonest.
corruption_paragraphs: Both biblical urgencies belong to powers that are losing. The Egyptians were urgent because they had been beaten; Nebuchadnezzar's commandment was urgent because he had been defied by three young men who would not argue with him. Neither urgency was a sign of strength, and neither accomplished what the urgent party intended — Egypt hurried out the people it had enslaved, and Babylon's haste killed its own executioners. That is worth holding when the world is at its most insistent. Pressure is not authority, and the volume of a demand is not a measure of its power.

The practical corruption is the tyranny of the urgent inside the church. Ministry is increasingly organized around whatever is pressing — the crisis, the deadline, the controversy of the week — and the slow work is displaced: catechizing children, visiting the dying, preparing sermons, praying. The three Hebrews give the pattern for resisting it, and the striking thing is how unhurried they are. They had settled the matter before the music played, they answer in a sentence, and they add but if not, refusing even to make their obedience contingent on rescue. Men who have settled the main thing in advance are very hard to stampede.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to press hard; Aramaic machtsephah, urgent, severe; Latin urgere, to press or drive.
roots_lines: Hebrew wattechezaq mitsrayim (H2388) — and Egypt was strong upon the people; Exodus 12:33, the same verb used of Pharaoh's hardened heart.
Aramaic machtsephah — urgent, harsh, severe; Daniel 3:22, of the king's commandment.
Aramaic 'azeh yattira — exceeding hot; the furnace heated seven times more than usual.
Hebrew chippazon (H2649) — haste, trepidation; the manner in which Israel was to eat the Passover.
Latin urgere — to press, drive; Webster's root, a force pushing rather than a clock running.
usage: “The Egyptians were urgent upon the people” — after ten plagues, they could not get them out fast enough.
“Because the king's commandment was urgent” — and the haste killed his own men.
“But if not” — the answer of men who had settled it beforehand.

pos: adv. (in the older English, urgently and perseveringly; with importunity — not, as now, immediately)
etymology: Latin instare, to stand upon, press upon, from in- and stare, to stand. The root sense is standing on a matter and not letting go. Modern English kept only the speed and lost the persistence.
biblical_def: This is one of the words modern readers most reliably misread. In the Authorized Version instantly does not mean at once; it means urgently, perseveringly, standing on the request. The elders of the Jews come on behalf of the centurion: “And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this” (Luk 7:4) — they pressed the case, they did not merely ask quickly. And Paul before Agrippa describes the whole worship of Israel: “Unto which promise our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come” (Act 26:7). Nothing about that is instantaneous — it is centuries of service, day and night, standing on a promise not yet received. The same root appears in the great command about prayer: “Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer” (Rom 12:12). To continue instant is to keep standing there. So the Bible's word for intensity is a word for endurance, and the modern loss is not merely lexical — a generation that reads instantly as immediately will hear every one of these verses as a promise of speed rather than a call to persist.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines instantly as immediately; without delay; and also with urgency or importunity, as in the Scripture use, they besought him instantly.
webster_full: IN'STANTLY, adv.
1. Immediately; without any intervening time; at the moment.
2. With urgent importunity.
And they besought him instantly. Luke 7.
IN'STANT, a. [L. instans, from insto, to press on; in and sto, to stand.]
Pressing; urgent; importunate; earnest. Continuing instant in prayer. Rom. 12.
scriptures: Acts 26:7
Unto which promise our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come. For which hope's sake, king Agrippa, I am accused of the Jews.
Luke 7:4
And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this:
Romans 12:12
Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer;
Luke 18:1
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;
corruption_summary: The word's drift from persevering to immediate mirrors the age exactly, and the church now expects of prayer what the English no longer means.
corruption_paragraphs: A believer who reads Romans 12:12 with the modern sense will conclude he is commanded to pray promptly. Paul is commanding him to stand on the matter and not leave. The difference is enormous in practice. Continuing instant in prayer is what the widow does before the unjust judge, what the Syrophenician woman does when she is refused twice, and what the twelve tribes were doing for centuries in Acts 26:7 — serving day and night toward a promise none of them lived to see fulfilled. Luke 18:1 gives the Lord's own purpose in teaching it: that men ought always to pray, and not to faint. The enemy of prayer in Scripture is not slowness; it is fainting.

The therapeutic and consumer instincts have made this worse by training Christians to evaluate prayer by response time. Where an answer is not quick, the conclusion drawn is that something is wrong — with the faith, the technique, or the request. Acts 26:7 describes generations of unanswered prayer offered by people who were counted faithful precisely for continuing. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds that God's timing is part of His answer, not an obstacle to it; and the older English preserved that instinct in a single adverb, which we have since spent.
roots_summary: Greek spoudaios (G4709), earnestly, diligently; en ekteneia (G1616), in intensity, stretched out; proskartereo (G4342), to persist obstinately in; Latin instare, to stand upon.
roots_lines: Greek en ekteneia (G1616) — in earnest intensity, stretched-out-ness; Acts 26:7, serving God day and night.
Greek spoudaios (G4709) — earnestly, with diligence; Luke 7:4, the elders pressing the centurion's case.
Greek proskarterountes (G4342) — persevering, holding fast to; Romans 12:12, continuing instant in prayer.
Greek me enkakein (G1573) — not to lose heart, not to faint; Luke 18:1, the opposite of continuing instant.
Latin instare, from in- and stare — to stand upon; Webster's root, where the persistence lives.
usage: “Instantly serving God day and night” — centuries of it, and not one moment of speed.
“They besought him instantly” — they pressed the case.
“Continuing instant in prayer” — the enemy is fainting, not slowness.

pos: adv. (with close scrutiny; with minute examination; closely)
etymology: From narrow, Saxon nearu, strait, close. To look narrowly is to look with the eye close in — the same figure as the English close inspection.
biblical_def: Both occurrences describe a searching examination, and in both the one examined would rather not be. Job complains of God's attention: “Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet” (Job 13:27). The picture is of a tracker following footprints, and Job experiences omniscience as surveillance — a man in the dark reads the same attribute as a threat that a man in the light reads as comfort. The second is the great taunt-song over the fallen king of Babylon: “They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms” (Isa 14:16). The dead crowd around and peer at him, leaning in to be sure it is really him. A tyrant who terrified the earth becomes an object of close inspection, and the verse is the answer to every accumulation of power. Set against Job's dread is David's invitation, which asks for the very thing Job resented: “Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts” (Psa 139:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines narrowly as with little breadth; contractedly; closely; accurately; with minute scrutiny; and nearly, within a little.
webster_full: NAR'ROWLY, adv.
1. With little breadth.
2. Contractedly; without much extent.
3. Closely; accurately; with minute scrutiny; as, to look narrowly into an affair.
Thou lookest narrowly unto all my paths. Job 13. 4. Nearly; within a little; by a small distance; as, he narrowly escaped.
scriptures: Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet.
Isaiah 14:16
They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms;
Psalm 139:23
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
Hebrews 4:13
Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
corruption_summary: Divine omniscience is experienced as surveillance and resented, or denied outright by open theism; Scripture presents it as the ground of both terror and comfort, depending on where a man stands.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 13:27 is honest about something devotional writing often avoids: being fully known is not automatically comforting. Job, in the dark and unable to account for his suffering, feels God's narrow looking as a man feels a tracker on his heels. The age has its own version, in which any absolute scrutiny is felt as a violation of autonomy, and the God who sees all is therefore an intolerable figure. Open theism offers the escape by denying exhaustive foreknowledge, and it is no escape at all — a God who does not know the end cannot be trusted with it, and Hebrews 4:13 is not negotiable: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.

What changes the experience is not the attribute but the standing. David asks for the identical scrutiny Job resents — search me, O God, and know my heart — because he is asking as a man in covenant, with nothing finally at stake in the verdict. That is the difference justification makes. And Isaiah 14:16 shows the attribute from the third side: the day comes when the men who could not be examined at all are looked at narrowly by everyone, and found to be very small. Omniscience is a terror to the guilty, a comfort to the covered, and a promise to everyone waiting for the tyrants to be seen plainly.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamar (H8104), to watch, keep, observe closely; shaqaph (H8259), to look down and gaze; chaqar (H2713), to search out.
roots_lines: Hebrew tishmor (H8104) — thou watchest, guardest, observest; Job 13:27, the tracker's attention on every path.
Hebrew yashgichu (H7688) — they shall gaze intently, peer; Isaiah 14:16, the dead leaning in to look.
Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, explore to the bottom; Psalm 139:23, invited rather than resented.
Hebrew tithaqqeh — thou settest a print, engravest; Job 13:27, of the mark on the heels.
Saxon nearu — strait, close; Webster's root, the eye brought close in.
usage: “Lookest narrowly unto all my paths” — omniscience felt as a tracker on the heels.
“They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee” — the tyrant, at last, inspected.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart” — the same attribute, invited.

pos: adv. (without fear or apprehension; in the older English, carelessly, without watchfulness)
etymology: Latin securus, from se-, without, and cura, care — literally without care. The old English sense is therefore not safe but unworried, which may be a virtue or a fatal negligence.
biblical_def: The Latin root matters: securus is without care, and the Authorized Version uses the adverb for people who are not looking over their shoulders — once innocently, once tragically. Solomon: “Devise not evil against thy neighbour, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee” (Pro 3:29). The neighbour's trust is itself the argument. He lives beside you without a guard because he assumes you are not plotting, and to exploit that assumption is the aggravation of the offence — the next verse adds, “Strive not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm” (Pro 3:30). Micah describes the same trust being robbed, and by the covenant people: “Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war” (Mic 2:8). The victims are travellers who were not expecting trouble, and the robbers are God's own people. Judges shows the other face of the word, where security is simple negligence: Laish dwelt careless and secure, with no magistrate in the land, and was destroyed (Jdg 18:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines securely as without fear or apprehension; carelessly; in an unguarded state; and notes that the Latin securus is without care.
webster_full: SECU'RELY, adv.
1. Without fear or apprehension; without care or anxiety.
His neighbor dwelleth securely by him. Prov. 3.
2. Carelessly; in an unguarded state.
SECU'RE, a. [L. securus; se, without, and cura, care.] Free from danger; safe; and also, careless; wanting caution.
scriptures: Proverbs 3:29
Devise not evil against thy neighbour, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee.
Micah 2:8
Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war.
Proverbs 3:30
Strive not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm.
Judges 18:7

Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people that were therein, how they dwelt careless, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure; and there was no magistrate in the land, that might put them to shame in any thing; and they were far from the Zidonians, and had no business with any man.
corruption_summary: Trust is now treated as a weakness that invites exploitation, so that the betrayal of it becomes the victim's fault.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 3:29 grounds a prohibition in the neighbour's defencelessness: do not devise evil against him seeing he dwelleth securely by thee. The modern instinct runs the other way — a man who did not lock the door, who trusted the wrong person, who failed to protect himself, is held partly responsible for what was done to him. Scripture puts the whole weight on the one who exploited the trust, and treats the trust itself as something owed protection rather than punished. That principle runs through the law's protection of the widow, the stranger, and the fatherless, and it is why the abuse of a trusted office is treated in Scripture as an aggravation, never a mitigation.

Micah 2:8 supplies the sharpest form of the charge, and the church should not read past it: the robbers are my people, stripping travellers who were averse from war — peaceable men who never expected it. Wolves inside the fold is not a modern discovery. And Judges 18:7 keeps the balance by showing the other sense of the word: Laish was quiet and secure with no magistrate in the land, and that carelessness was ruin. The dictionary holds both — trust is a good that the trustworthy must guard, and the absence of any lawful authority is not peace but an invitation.
roots_summary: Hebrew betach (H983), securely, in confidence; batach (H982), to trust; shoqet (H8252), quiet, undisturbed; Latin securus, without care.
roots_lines: Hebrew lavetach (H983) — in confidence, securely; Proverbs 3:29, the neighbour living without a guard.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to lean upon; the root, and the standard word for trusting in the LORD.
Hebrew shuve milchamah — turned back from war, averse from war; Micah 2:8, the peaceable travellers robbed.
Hebrew shoqet uvoteach (H8252, H982) — quiet and secure; Judges 18:7, of Laish before its destruction.
Latin se- and cura — without care; Webster's root, which is why security can mean safety or negligence.
usage: “Seeing he dwelleth securely by thee” — his trust is the reason, not the excuse.
“Them that pass by securely as men averse from war” — and the robbers are my people.
“Quiet and secure; and there was no magistrate in the land” — the other sense, and it was ruin.

pos: adv. (fully; entirely; completely; to the end of the matter)
etymology: From thorough, an older form of through, Saxon thurh. To do a thing thoroughly is to go through it — not to stop partway. The Authorized Version often spells it throughly.
biblical_def: The word marks completeness, and Scripture applies it to two very different obligations. The first is restitution in the civil law: a man who injures another in a quarrel “shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed” (Exo 21:19). The obligation does not end when the offender has been punished or has apologized; it ends when the injured man is well and his lost wages are made up. Biblical justice is not satisfied by penalty alone; it is satisfied by the victim being made whole. The second is reformation, and there it means leaving nothing standing: when Athaliah fell, “all the people of the land went into the house of Baal, and brake it down; his altars and his images brake they in pieces thoroughly, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars” (2Ki 11:18). Half-measures in reformation are the standing failure of the good kings of Judah, of whom it is repeatedly said that the high places were not taken away. The same completeness is required of the minister: Scripture is given “that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works” (2Ti 3:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thoroughly as fully; entirely; completely; and notes that thorough is from through, signifying passing quite through a thing.
webster_full: THOR'OUGHLY, adv. thur'oly.
Fully; entirely; completely; as, to be thoroughly scared.
Let the medicine operate thoroughly.
THOR'OUGH, a. thur'o. [a different orthography of through.]
1. Literally, passing through or to the end; hence, complete; perfect; as a thorough reformation. He shall cause him to be thoroughly healed. Ex. 21.
scriptures: Exodus 21:19
If he rise again, and walk abroad upon his staff, then shall he that smote him be quit: only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed.
2 Kings 11:18

And all the people of the land went into the house of Baal, and brake it down; his altars and his images brake they in pieces thoroughly, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest appointed officers over the house of the LORD.
2 Timothy 3:17
That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Repentance is treated as complete when it is confessed, and reformation as complete when it is announced — and Exodus 21:19 will not allow either.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 21:19 is a verse the church needs and rarely preaches. The man who did the harm pays for the lost time and sees the injured man thoroughly healed. Apology is not named; restitution is. A great deal of contemporary teaching on forgiveness runs the other way, placing the whole burden on the injured party to release the offender while nothing is required of the offender beyond remorse. Scripture does command forgiveness, and it also commands restitution, and Zacchaeus is the New Testament proof that the second survives into the gospel era: he restored fourfold, and salvation came to his house that day.

2 Kings 11:18 gives the same principle in reformation. The house of Baal was not regulated, licensed, or gradually phased out; it was broken down and its images broken thoroughly. The recurring epitaph on otherwise good kings of Judah — howbeit the high places were not taken away — is Scripture's own commentary on partial reform. A man who deals thoroughly with an idol does not have to keep dealing with it, and this is the pastoral wisdom behind the Puritan practice of mortification: sin is not managed at a tolerable level but put to death. 2 Timothy 3:17 supplies the equipment for it, and the equipment is the whole of Scripture.
roots_summary: Hebrew rappo yerappe (H7495), healing he shall heal; heytev (H3190), to do well, thoroughly; Greek exartizo (G1822), to fit out completely; Saxon thurh, through.
roots_lines: Hebrew rappo yerappe (H7495) — healing he shall cause to be healed; Exodus 21:19, the doubled verb rendered thoroughly healed.
Hebrew heytev (H3190) — to do a thing well and completely; 2 Kings 11:18, of the images broken in pieces.
Greek exertismenos (G1822) — completely equipped, fitted out; 2 Timothy 3:17, of the man of God.
Greek artios (G739) — fitted, complete; the adjective perfect in the same verse.
Saxon thurh — through; Webster's root, and the reason the Authorized Version often spells it throughly.
usage: “Shall cause him to be thoroughly healed” — the obligation ends when the man is well.
“Brake they in pieces thoroughly” — and the high places usually were not.
“Throughly furnished unto all good works” — equipped by the whole of Scripture.

etymology: From scarce, Old French escars, sparing, from Late Latin excarpsus. To do a thing scarcely is to do it barely, with difficulty, and nearly not at all.
biblical_def: Two occurrences, and both are arguments from difficulty. Paul measures the love of God by a human scale and finds the scale far too short: “For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die” (Rom 5:7). Men hardly ever die for the righteous; occasionally one might for a genuinely good man. And then the contrast: “But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom 5:8). Not for the righteous, not for the good, but for sinners — the one category no man dies for. Peter's use runs the other way, as a warning: “And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1Pe 4:18), quoting Proverbs 11:31. The scarcely there does not question the certainty of salvation; it describes its difficulty — what it cost, and the fire the saved pass through. Peter has just been writing about fiery trial. If the way home is that hard for those who are being saved, the position of those who are not is unspeakable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scarcely as hardly; with difficulty; and scarce as not plentiful; being in small quantity in proportion to the demand.
webster_full: SC'ARCELY, adv.
1. Hardly; with difficulty.
Slowly he sails, and scarcely stems the tides.
We scarcely could persuade ourselves of the fact.
2. Hardly; scantily. Scarcely for a righteous man will one die. Rom. 5. From escars, sparing, niggardly.
scriptures: Romans 5:7
For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die.
Romans 5:8
But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
1 Peter 4:18
And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?
Proverbs 11:31
Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner.
corruption_summary: God's love is presented as a response to something lovable in man, which destroys the entire force of Paul's scarcely.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common misstatement of the gospel in our time is that God loves us because He sees our worth. Romans 5:7-8 was written to make that reading impossible. Paul sets up the best case human love can produce — a man might peradventure die for a genuinely good man — and then says God's love went where human love never goes: while we were yet sinners. If the object had been lovable, the demonstration would prove nothing. The word commendeth means God is exhibiting His love, putting it on display, and the display depends entirely on the unworthiness of those it fell upon. Self-worth preaching does not make this gospel warmer; it removes the thing that made it astonishing.

1 Peter 4:18 guards the opposite flank, against a cheapness that treats salvation as easy and therefore small. The righteous are scarcely saved — not doubtfully, for God keeps His own, but at enormous cost and through fire. Peter is writing to people under persecution and telling them the narrowness of the way is not a sign that something has gone wrong. The Reformed hold both without contradiction: salvation is certain because it rests on God's decree and Christ's finished work, and it is difficult because the road runs through a world at war with it. Certainty of arrival is not a promise of an easy passage.
roots_summary: Greek molis (G3433), with difficulty, hardly; sunistemi (G4921), to commend, to set together and display; Old French escars, sparing.
roots_lines: Greek molis (G3433) — with difficulty, scarcely; Romans 5:7, of dying for a righteous man.
Greek molis sozetai (G3433, G4982) — is scarcely saved; 1 Peter 4:18, of the righteous passing through fire.
Greek sunistesin (G4921) — He commends, exhibits, sets forth for display; Romans 5:8, God putting His love on show.
Greek hamartolon onton hemon (G268) — while we were sinners; the state, not the potential, that the love fell upon.
Old French escars — sparing, niggardly; Webster's root behind scarce.
usage: “Scarcely for a righteous man will one die” — the best human love can manage.
“While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” — where human love never goes.
“If the righteous scarcely be saved” — certain, and costly.

pos: adv. (without difficulty; readily; with little resistance)
etymology: From easy, Old French aisie, at ease. In both Authorized Version occurrences the adverb marks something that happens too readily — a provocation taken quickly, and a sin that fastens without effort.
biblical_def: Both occurrences describe a readiness that is a fault. The first is in the great chapter on charity: love “doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil” (1Co 13:5). The measure of love here is a slowness to take offence — not an inability to be wronged but an unreadiness to be triggered by it, set among the other marks of a love that does not keep accounts. The second is the running metaphor of Hebrews: “let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1). Two things go: every weight, which need not be sinful at all, and the sin which easily besets — the Greek pictures a garment that wraps close about the legs. A runner strips because things that are fine at rest are ruinous at speed. Then the writer names what makes the stripping possible: “Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Heb 12:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines easily as without difficulty or great labor; without pain or anxiety; readily; without reluctance; and without shaking or jolting.
webster_full: E'ASILY, adv. s as z.
1. Without difficulty or great labor; without great exertion, or great expense of labor or money.
2. Without pain, anxiety or disturbance; as, to pass life well and easily.
3. Readily; without the pain of reluctance.
Not easily provoked. 1 Cor. 13. 4. Smoothly; quietly; gently; without tumult or discord. 5. Without violent shaking or jolting.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 13:5
Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
Hebrews 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Hebrews 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
1 Corinthians 13:4
Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
corruption_summary: Being easily provoked is now a credential — proof that one cares — and the besetting sin is renamed an identity rather than a garment to be laid aside.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 13:5 is unfashionable in a culture where readiness to take offence is treated as moral seriousness. To be quickly provoked signals that one has convictions; to be slow signals indifference. Paul lists it as a failure of love, alongside seeking one's own and thinking evil, and the surrounding verses make clear he is not describing a placid temperament but a disciplined one — charity suffereth long, which presumes there is something to suffer. The man who is not easily provoked is not the man who has not been wronged; he is the man who has been wronged and has not kept the account.

Hebrews 12:1 is corrupted in a subtler way. The besetting sin — the one that wraps close and trips a man at speed — is increasingly described as a fixed identity rather than a garment. Once a pattern of sin is understood as who a man is, laying it aside becomes unthinkable and even cruel to suggest. The runner's metaphor says the opposite: the thing clings closely, it is not the runner, and it comes off. Notice also that every weight goes too, and weights are not sins — they are lawful things that cost speed. Sanctification involves putting down more than what is forbidden, and it is sustained not by self-scrutiny but by looking to the One who ran first.
roots_summary: Greek paroxuno (G3947), to sharpen, provoke to anger; euperistatos (G2139), easily surrounding, closely clinging; ogkos (G3591), a bulk or weight.
roots_lines: Greek ou paroxunetai (G3947) — is not sharpened, not provoked; 1 Corinthians 13:5, the root of English paroxysm.
Greek euperistaton (G2139) — easily surrounding, standing well around; Hebrews 12:1, of a garment clinging to the legs.
Greek ogkos (G3591) — bulk, mass, weight; the thing laid aside that is not itself a sin.
Greek hupomone (G5281) — patience, endurance under load; the manner of the running.
Greek aphorontes (G872) — looking away from everything else unto; Hebrews 12:2, the fixed gaze that makes the stripping possible.
usage: “Is not easily provoked” — listed as a failure of love, not a lack of conviction.
“The sin which doth so easily beset us” — a garment round the legs, not an identity.
“Every weight” — lawful things that still cost speed.

pos: adv. (in a straight line or course; without deviation; straight toward)
etymology: Latin directus, straight, from dirigere, to set straight, from di- and regere, to rule or guide. The word is about a line, not about speed; modern English has added the sense of at once.
biblical_def: Both occurrences are architectural and ritual, and both concern the direction a thing faces. The first is the ordinance of the red heifer: “And Eleazar the priest shall take of her blood with his finger, and sprinkle of her blood directly before the tabernacle of the congregation seven times” (Num 19:4). The blood is not sprinkled anywhere convenient; it is sprinkled directly before the tabernacle, on a straight line toward the dwelling of God, seven times. The heifer was burned outside the camp and its ashes mixed with water for the purifying of the unclean — the ordinance Hebrews cites when arguing from the lesser to the greater: “For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh” (Heb 9:13). The second occurrence is in Ezekiel's temple vision, describing a door in the head of the way, “even the way directly before the wall toward the east, as one entereth into them” (Eze 42:12). In both places the point is orientation: the sacrifice faces the sanctuary, and the way faces the wall. Approach to God in Scripture is never approximate; it is aimed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines directly as in a straight line or course; rectilineally; and immediately; without delay — the first being the older and primary sense.
webster_full: DIRECT'LY, adv.
1. In a straight line or course; rectilineally; not in a winding course.
Aim directly at the mark.
2. Immediately; soon; without delay; as, he will be with you directly.
3. Openly; expressly; without circumlocution or ambiguity. Sprinkle of her blood directly before the tabernacle. Num. 19. From directus, from dirigo, to make straight.
scriptures: Numbers 19:4
And Eleazar the priest shall take of her blood with his finger, and sprinkle of her blood directly before the tabernacle of the congregation seven times:
Ezekiel 42:12
And according to the doors of the chambers that were toward the south was a door in the head of the way, even the way directly before the wall toward the east, as one entereth into them.
Hebrews 9:13
For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh:
Hebrews 9:14
How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
corruption_summary: The precision of Israel's ritual is dismissed as primitive fussiness, when it is the very thing the New Testament argues from.
corruption_paragraphs: Chapters like Numbers 19 are commonly skipped, and where they are read the exactness is treated as the anthropology of an ancient people — taboo, ritual purity, the usual apparatus. The writer to the Hebrews does something else with it entirely: he takes the ordinance as valid, effective in its own order, and then argues upward. If the ashes of an heifer sanctified to the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ purge the conscience (Heb 9:13-14). The whole argument collapses if the heifer was superstition. The precision was God's, and it was teaching a nation that access is real, costly, and exactly specified — blood sprinkled directly before the tabernacle, seven times, with nothing left to preference.

The application is the regulative principle, and it is where the dictionary has always stood. If God cared which direction a priest faced while sprinkling, the notion that He is indifferent to what is done in Christian worship cannot be sustained. What has changed with the new covenant is not God's particularity but the ordinances He has appointed: preaching, prayer, singing, baptism, and the Supper, with the sacrifices fulfilled and finished in Christ. The believer now comes boldly, which is a greater access than Eleazar ever had — and he comes by a way as exactly specified as the old one, through one Mediator and no other.
roots_summary: Hebrew nokach (H5227), straight in front of, over against; parah adummah (H6510), the red heifer; Latin dirigere, to set straight.
roots_lines: Hebrew el nokach penei ohel mo'ed (H5227) — straight toward the face of the tent of meeting; Numbers 19:4.
Hebrew parah adummah (H6510, H122) — the red heifer, without spot and never yoked; Numbers 19:2.
Hebrew derekh (H1870) — a way, road; Ezekiel 42:12, the way directly before the wall.
Greek spodos damaleos (G4700, G1151) — ashes of a heifer; Hebrews 9:13, the ordinance argued from.
Latin dirigere, from regere — to set straight, to rule; Webster's root, a line before it is a clock.
usage: “Sprinkle of her blood directly before the tabernacle… seven times” — aimed, and counted.
“The way directly before the wall toward the east” — orientation, in Ezekiel's temple.
“How much more shall the blood of Christ” — the argument needs the heifer to have been real.

pos: adv. (concisely; in few words; in short)
etymology: From brief, Latin brevis, short. In Romans the adverb does not mean hastily but summed up — the whole law gathered into a single sentence without any of it being lost.
biblical_def: Twice, and each is a lesson in compression. Paul, having listed four commandments of the second table, writes: “and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Rom 13:9). Briefly comprehended — the Greek is a word from accounting, to sum up under one head. The commandments are not abolished by the summary; they are totalled by it, which is why Paul has just quoted four of them individually and why he adds, “Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law” (Rom 13:10). The summary tells you what the particulars are for; the particulars tell you what the summary means. The second occurrence is Peter closing his first epistle: “By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, as I suppose, I have written briefly, exhorting, and testifying that this is the true grace of God wherein ye stand” (1Pe 5:12). Five chapters on suffering, submission, eldership and the devil, and the apostle calls it brief — and states its whole purpose in a clause: that they should know the ground they were standing on was the true grace of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines briefly as concisely; in few words; and brief as short; concise; contracted.
webster_full: BRIEF'LY, adv.
Concisely; in few words; in short.
Let me briefly state the case.
BRIEF, a. [Fr. bref; L. brevis.] Short; concise; contracted; as a brief discourse.
It is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself. Rom. 13.
scriptures: Romans 13:9

For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
1 Peter 5:12
By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, as I suppose, I have written briefly, exhorting, and testifying that this is the true grace of God wherein ye stand.
Romans 13:10
Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
Matthew 22:40
On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
corruption_summary: The summary is used to abolish the particulars, so that love becomes a licence to set aside the commandments it was supposed to total.
corruption_paragraphs: The love-summary of Romans 13:9 is now routinely deployed to overrule the law it summarizes: since love fulfils the law, any conduct a man sincerely calls loving is held to satisfy it. Paul makes that impossible by quoting the commandments in the same sentence. He does not replace Thou shalt not commit adultery with love thy neighbour; he says the second sums the first. An accountant's total does not delete the line items — it depends on them, and a total that contradicts its entries is simply wrong. Wherever love is invoked to license what the Decalogue forbids, the summary has been detached from what it sums, and the result is not a higher ethic but a vacancy.

The opposite error is a legalism that multiplies particulars and never arrives at the heart, which the Lord rebuked in men who tithed mint and anise. Matthew 22:40 gives the structure: on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets — hang, as a door hangs on hinges, needing both. And Peter's brevity is worth the ministers' attention. Five chapters he calls brief, written to tell a suffering church what ground it stood on. Brevity in Scripture is never thinness; it is compression, and compression is what a man can carry into a fire.
roots_summary: Greek anakephalaioo (G346), to sum up under one head; di oligon (G3641), by few words; kephalaion (G2774), a sum, chief point; Latin brevis, short.
roots_lines: Greek anakephalaioutai (G346) — is summed up under one head; Romans 13:9, an accounting term, not a replacement.
Greek kephalaion (G2774) — a sum, the chief point; the noun behind the verb, a total gathered at the head of a column.
Greek di oligon (G3641) — through few things, briefly; 1 Peter 5:12.
Greek pleroma nomou (G4138) — the fulfilling, the fulness of the law; Romans 13:10.
Latin brevis — short; Webster's root, and the source of English abbreviate.
usage: “Briefly comprehended in this saying” — a total, quoted alongside its line items.
“Love worketh no ill to his neighbour” — which is how you know what the summary means.
“I have written briefly” — five chapters, and he calls it short.
